title: Why the Sky Is Blue
idea: Tiny air molecules scatter short blue light waves in every direction while long red waves pass straight through

segments.narration: Sunlight is white, so why is the sky blue?
segments.visual_directive: A clean white beam sweeps across a dark background, then hard cuts to a bright blue dome sky.

segments.narration: Sunlight looks white, but it's really every color mixed together. When that light hits our air, the colors split. Blue goes everywhere, red doesn't.
segments.visual_directive: A white light bar fans out into a rainbow spectrum, then the view pulls back to Earth with a thin glowing atmosphere layer.

segments.narration: Picture one sunbeam hitting tiny air molecules. They're way smaller than light waves, so they scatter short waves best. Blue light has a tiny, choppy wave. It slams into a molecule and bounces everywhere. Up, down, sideways. Red light has a long, smooth wave. It mostly slips straight past. So blue gets scattered from every patch of sky into your eyes. You're seeing scattered blue from all directions at once.
segments.visual_directive: Close-up motion graphics of one beam hitting glowing air dots. Short blue zigzag waves bounce in all directions while long red waves glide straight through, tinting the background blue.

segments.narration: Sunsets turn red because blue's already scattered away. Only straight red survives. That white sunlight is what makes the sky blue.
segments.visual_directive: The blue sky shifts to a low orange sunset with red rays reaching the viewer, then resets to the opening white beam.
